goals.lickLoop3: In bars 1 and 3 play the box 1 licks, in bars 2 and 4 answer with your own phrase.
goals.lickLoop12: Over Am and C play the licks that land on the third; over Em and D land on the third with your own phrase.
goals.stdJazzBlues: A 12-bar blues with added ii–Vs. The blues scale of the key holds it together; at the changes aim for the thirds and sevenths of the chords.
goals.stdMinorBlues: The minor pentatonic of the key fits the whole form. Over the two dominants in bars 9–10 aim for chord tones.
goals.stdAutumn: A ii–V–I in major, followed by a ii–V–i in the relative minor. One major scale is enough; only over the dominant before the minor chord play its third, which is not in the scale.
goals.stdRhythm: The chord changes every two beats. Start with roots only, then add thirds and join them into lines.
goals.stdCycle: A ii–V–I in twelve keys, each a fourth above the previous one. Carry the same idea from key to key.
goals.stdCycleLabel: ii–V–I around the circle of fourths
goals.stdBlueBossa: The C minor pentatonic or C minor scale fits the first eight bars. In bars 9–12 the key briefly jumps to Db major: play the Db major scale there, then return to C minor.
goals.stdATrain: Everything is in C major except the D7 in bars 3–4: over it raise F to F#, the third of D7.
goals.stdAllThings: The chords move around the circle of fourths, and near the end the key changes from Ab major to C major. Lead a line through thirds and sevenths, moving at most a half step at each change.
goals.stdAllThingsLabel: All the Things You Are (A section)
goals.stdSoWhat: D Dorian for 16 bars, then the same scale a half step up (Eb Dorian) for 8, and back. Few chords, so build phrases and leave space.
goals.stdPopAxis: I–V–vi–IV, the progression behind hundreds of pop songs. The C major (or A minor) pentatonic fits all of it; end phrases on chord tones.
goals.stdFifties: The 1950s progression (I–vi–IV–V). Play the G major scale and aim for each chord's root on beat one.
goals.stdAndalusian: The Andalusian cadence walks down from Am to E. The A minor scale fits the first three chords; over E play G# instead of G (Phrygian dominant).
goals.targetThird: Land on the chord's third at each change — Am→C, C→E, Em→G, D→F#.
goals.targetFifth: Land on the chord's fifth — Am→E, C→G, Em→B, D→A.
goals.voiceLeading: Before the change, play the common tone or a step next to a note of the next chord (Gm→Bbm: shared Bb; Gm→Cm: shared G).
goals.switchingKeys: Halfway through the loop the key moves from G to B — shift your lines (scales/arpeggios) to the new key.
goals.tritoneNormal: Resolve G7 to C — the third of G7 (B) rises a half step to C, the seventh (F) falls a half step to E.
goals.tritoneSubV: Over Db7 emphasize the third (F) and the seventh (Cb = B), then resolve them by half step: F→E, B→C.
goals.secondaryDominants: After each secondary dominant, land on the third of the next chord.
goals.borrowedBackdoor: Over Fm7 play F dorian, over Bb7 play Bb Lydian dominant (or Bb mixolydian), then step into a chord tone of C.
goals.triads: Play only triads over the loop — move each chord to its closest inversion instead of jumping shapes.
goals.pentatonicBox1: Improvise using box 1 only (frets 5–8) — your first real improvisation.
goals.majorC: Phrase with the C major scale and end your lines on the note C.
goals.pentatonicBoxes: With each loop, move to the neighbouring pentatonic box.
goals.modeCharacteristic: Emphasize the mode's characteristic note over the backing.
goals.pentThenMode: Play four bars with the minor pentatonic only, then for the next four add the two notes that turn it into Dorian. Listen to what changes.
goals.approachBelow: Just before the chord changes, play the note a half step below the new chord's root and land on the root on beat one: G#→A, B→C, D#→E, C#→D.
goals.approachBelowLabel: Level 5: a half step from below
goals.approachEnclosure: Surround the target: a half step above, a half step below, the root on beat one: Bb–G#→A, Db–B→C, F–D#→E, Eb–C#→D.
goals.approachThirdBelow: Approach the third of each chord from a half step below and land on it on beat one: E→F (Dm7), A#→B (G7), D#→E (Cmaj7).
goals.approachThirdEnclosure: Surround the third: Gb–E→F (Dm7), C–A#→B (G7), F–D#→E (Cmaj7).
goals.limitThreeNotes: Play with only three notes of box 1: A, C and D. All your attention goes to rhythm and phrase length.
goals.limitOneString: Play on the G string only: A minor pentatonic sits there on frets 0, 2, 5, 7, 9 and 12. The phrase comes from moving along the neck.
goals.limitRhythm: Play every phrase with the same rhythm: a quarter note, two eighths, a half note. Change the notes, keep the rhythm.
goals.bluesMinorPent: Play the whole blues with the minor pentatonic from the key's root. It sounds raw because its minor third rubs against the dominant chord.
goals.bluesMajorPent: Play the whole blues with the major pentatonic: the same box shape three frets lower. It sounds brighter because it has the chord's major third.
goals.bluesMixedPent: Change colour with the chord: major pentatonic over the I chord, minor over IV and V.
goals.pedalModes: The root stays in the bass and the variant changes the mode. Play slowly and rest on the notes that set this mode apart from the others.
goals.chordScaleCharacteristic: On every chord, play its characteristic tone from the hinted scale.
goals.arpeggiosOnly: Play chord arpeggios only — outline the harmony.
goals.targetRoot: Land on the chord's root at each change — Am→A, C→C, Em→E, D→D.
goals.targetSeventh: Land on the chord's seventh — Am7→G, Cmaj7→B, Em7→D, D7→C.
goals.targetAny: No fixed target: land on any chord tone you hear — your first free improvisation.
goals.voiceLeadingThirdsSevenths: Voice the thirds and sevenths smoothly: F→F→E or C→B→B through Dm7–G7–Cmaj7.
goals.switchingKeysEasy: Halfway through the loop the key moves from C to F major. One note changes (B becomes Bb) — switch scales when the hint shows the new key.
goals.tritoneVideo: Chromatic bass descent: Bm7–Bb7–Am7–Ab7–Gmaj7. Bb7 and Ab7 are tritone substitutes of the dominants.
goals.borrowedDiatonic: The diatonic road to C: Dm7–G7. Compare its sound with the backdoor.
goals.melodicMinor67: Emphasize the 6 (F#) and the major 7 (G#) over both Am chords.
goals.melodicMinorHints: Use the melodic-minor hint shown on each chord.
goals.harmonicMinorGSharp: Over E7 emphasize G# — the characteristic note of A harmonic minor.
goals.harmonicMinorPhrygian: Over E7 play E Phrygian dominant (from A harmonic minor).

goals.giantStepsPattern: Play a 1-2-3-5 pattern of each chord through the form.
goals.giantStepsArps: Play chord arpeggios through the whole form.
goals.bluesBox1: 12-bar blues in A — improvise in pentatonic box 1.
goals.bluesChordTones: 12-bar blues in A — land on a chord tone at every change.
goals.playRest: Play only in bars marked “play”. In “rest” bars play nothing: listen to the backing and plan the next phrase.
goals.callResponse: Two bars of question, two bars of answer. Start the answer with a motif from the question and end it on a chord tone.
goals.playRestLabel: Play a bar, rest a bar
goals.bluesRoots: On beat one of every bar play the root of the chord: A over A7, D over D7, E over E7.
goals.bluesRootsQuick: As above, but with a quick change: bar 2 is D7, so play D there.
goals.bluesRiff: Play the boogie riff through the whole form. Move it with the chord and keep the long and short eighths.
goals.bluesComping: Comp: two strums a bar, or just the thirds and sevenths on the D and G strings.
goals.bluesLickLoop: In bars 1, 5 and 9 play the named lick. In the others answer with your own phrase or leave a rest.
goals.bluesAAB: Bars 1–2: a phrase. Bars 5–6: the same phrase again. Bars 9–10: the answer. Do not play in the other bars.
goals.bluesMotif: Pick one short rhythm and play the whole chorus with it. Change only the notes.
goals.bluesBoxes: Change area of the neck every four bars, following the cue. Make the move with a slide along one string.
goals.bluesTurnaround: Improvise for 10 bars, then play a turnaround in bars 11–12 and end on a note of E7.
goals.bluesTargetRoot: On beat one of every bar land on the root of the chord: A, D or E.
goals.bluesTargetThird: On beat one of every bar land on the third of the chord: C# over A7, F# over D7, G# over E7.
goals.bluesTargetSeventh: On beat one of every bar land on the seventh of the chord: G over A7, C over D7, D over E7.
goals.bluesApproach: Just before beat one play the note a half step below the chord's third and land on the third: C→C#, F→F#, G→G#.
goals.bluesGuideTones: On beat one play the third or the seventh of the chord. Look for half-step moves: C#→C and G→F# when A7 changes to D7.
goals.bluesJazzThirds: On every chord change land on the chord's third. Between the changes connect the thirds with the F blues scale.
goals.formStandard: The plain 12-bar form. Play what the modules taught you.
goals.formQuick: Quick change: bar 2 is the IV chord. Mark that change with a note of D7.
goals.formSlow: Slow blues in 12/8. Play fewer notes, longer phrases and slow bends.
goals.formMinor: Minor blues. The minor pentatonic fits the whole form; over F7 and E7 in bars 9–10 aim for chord tones.
goals.formEight: The eight-bar form: the V chord arrives in the second bar and the last two bars are a turnaround.
goals.formSixteen: The sixteen-bar form: eight bars on the I chord, then the second half of a regular blues.
goals.triadsComp: Comp with triads only on the given string set. At each change take the voicing shown on the board, the nearest to the previous one.
goals.triadsOnePosition: Play the whole progression in one place on the neck: every chord as a triad on strings 2-3-4, moving your hand no more than two frets.
goals.vlPopAxis: C–G–Am–F with triads by the shortest way. On beat one of each chord play its top voice.
goals.vlTwoFiveOne: Dm–G–C with triads. Notice which notes stay at each change.
goals.vlAndalusian: Am–G–F–E: the top voice walks down by step. Play it on beat one of each chord.
goals.vlCycle: The whole cycle of fourths with triads on strings 1-2-3, each voicing nearest to the previous one.
goals.triadTonesOnly: Over each chord play only the notes of its triad. On beat one of every bar play one of them.
goals.triadTopMelody: Play only the highest note of the voicing shown on the board. Together they form the melody of the progression.
goals.triadPairs: Over Am7 play the notes of the F triad (F A C) and the G triad (G B D) in turn. Start the groups on different notes.
goals.shells251: Play Dm7–G7–Cmaj7 with shell voicings, four short strokes to the bar. Take the voicing shown on the board; your hand hardly moves.
goals.shellsBlues: The whole jazz blues with shell voicings, four strokes to the bar. On the quick changes play two strokes per chord.
goals.drop2TwoFiveOne: ii–V–I with drop 2 voicings nearest to the previous one. On beat one of each chord play its top voice, then the rest of the voicing.
goals.guideTonesBlues: Play only the third and seventh of each chord on the D and G strings. Notice that at each change one note stays and the other moves a half step.
goals.guideTonesCycle: Thirds and sevenths through ii–V–I in every key. Start slowly and do not jump around the neck.
goals.compFourToTheBar: Four short, even strokes to the bar, accented on 2 and 4. The chords should sound like a drum with pitch.
goals.compBossa: Comp Blue Bossa in a bossa rhythm with drop 2 voicings. Stay with the rhythmic pattern of the backing.
goals.compStandards: Comp with the drop 2 voicings shown on the board, in a swing feel. On beat one of each chord play its top voice.

e-string-notes.name: Notes of the E string
e-string-notes.theory: Improvisation starts with knowing the fretboard. Step one is the low E string (6th string): from fret 0 to 12 the notes run chromatically — E F F# G G# A A# B C C# D D# E. Once you know it by heart, you can find the root of a scale or chord quickly, because most shapes start on this string. Practice both directions: see a fret and name the note, then read a name and find the fret.

key-signatures.name: Key Signatures
key-signatures.theory: A key tells you which notes “live at home”. The circle of fifths orders the keys: moving clockwise adds sharps (C→G→D→A→E→B), counter-clockwise adds flats (C→F→Bb→Eb→Ab). Accidentals always join in the same order (sharps: F#, C#, G#, D#…; flats: Bb, Eb, Ab, Db…), so a key's position on the circle tells you at once which notes are altered. When a bandmate says “play in D”, the key signature is what makes that unambiguous. In improvisation this is step one: the key signature tells you which seven notes you can build a solo from in a given tune.

pentatonic-scale.name: Pentatonic Scale
pentatonic-scale.theory: The minor pentatonic (1 b3 4 5 b7) is most players’ first improvising language: it sounds right in blues, rock and folk. Box 1 (e.g. A minor at frets 5–8) sits comfortably under the fingers, so you can focus on phrasing instead of finding notes. Box 2 starts on the minor third and extends the scale up the neck. Switch keys with the selector: the shape stays the same and just slides along the neck. Play with a metronome, up and down, evenly in time. Every box is made of two shapes that alternate: a rectangle (two adjacent strings, notes 3 frets apart) and a stack (three adjacent strings, 2 frets apart); between the G and B strings everything shifts by one fret. The idea comes from the Fret Science lesson “Two Simple Shapes UNLOCK the Pentatonic Scale”.

major-scale.name: Major Scale
major-scale.theory: The major scale (1 2 3 4 5 6 7) is the reference point for everything that follows: modes, chord construction and harmony are all described against it. A one-position box, two or three notes per string, lays the whole scale out as a repeatable pattern. Play it up and down with a metronome, then in thirds and fourths — that is when the scale starts sounding like melody rather than an exercise.

fretboard-notes.name: Notes of the Rest of the Fretboard
fretboard-notes.term: Notes of the Rest of the Fretboard
fretboard-notes.theory: Now you extend the map to every string. Neighbouring strings E–A–D–G–B are a perfect fourth apart (5 semitones), with one exception: G to B is a major third (4 semitones). So the note at fret 5 of one string is the next open string (on the G string, fret 4). The goal is to see every note anywhere in frets 1–12; without that, following the changes higher up the neck is guesswork.

pentatonic-positions.name: Pentatonic Scale Positions
pentatonic-positions.theory: The five boxes are one scale — G minor pentatonic (G, Bb, C, D, F) — spread over the whole neck. Each box starts on the next note of that scale. The video names the boxes after their starting note: G minor pent (fret 3), Bb major pent (fret 5), C dorian pent (fret 7), D phrygian pent (fret 10), F mixolydian pent (fret 12). Every box uses the same five notes; only the shape under your fingers changes. Learn the boxes one by one, then connect neighbours.

modes.name: Modes
modes.theory: Modes are the seven scales you get by starting the major scale on each degree: I Ionian, II Dorian, III Phrygian, IV Lydian, V Mixolydian, VI Aeolian, VII Locrian. Compared with the major scale on the same root, Dorian has b3 and b7, Phrygian b2 b3 b6 b7, Lydian #4, Mixolydian b7, Aeolian b3 b6 b7 and Locrian b2 b3 b5 b6 b7. Each mode has a characteristic note that sets it apart from plain major or minor: the major sixth in Dorian, b2 in Phrygian, #4 in Lydian, b7 in Mixolydian. Emphasize those notes when you want the mode to be heard. A practical shortcut: a mode is a pentatonic from the same root plus two notes (Fret Science lesson “Stop Memorizing Modes”).

chord-construction.name: How Chords Are Built
chord-construction.theory: Chords come from the scale: stack every other note (1-3-5) from a scale degree. In F major: F-A-C is degree I (major), G-Bb-D is ii (minor), E-G-Bb is vii (diminished). You recognize a triad type by its distances: major third + perfect fifth = major, minor third + perfect fifth = minor, minor third + diminished fifth = dim, major third + augmented fifth = aug. The same stacking extends to seventh chords and every extension used in improvisation.

chord-scale-major.name: Chord/Scale Relationships (Major)
chord-scale-major.theory: Every chord in a key has “its” mode. In C major: Cmaj7 → Ionian, Dm7 → Dorian (Dm13 is the same chord with extensions), Em7 → Phrygian, Fmaj7 → Lydian (hence the #11 in Fmaj7#11), G7 → Mixolydian, Am7 → Aeolian, Bm7b5 → Locrian. In practice you play the notes of the key, but on each chord you aim at its characteristic note. This is the first step from “playing in the key” to “following the changes”.

triads.name: Triads
triads.theory: Triads on the top three strings (G-B-E) are the most economical way to see harmony on the neck. Each chord has three inversions sitting next to each other, so a chord change means moving your fingers a fret or two. The same shapes work for comping and as targets for melodic lines. Also drill the intervals: major 1 3 5, minor 1 b3 5, diminished 1 b3 b5, augmented 1 3 #5.

arpeggios.name: Arpeggios
arpeggios.theory: An arpeggio is a chord played one note at a time. It contains only chord tones, so it always fits over that chord — the safest material when chords keep changing. The diagrams show each arpeggio across all six strings in one position: 1 b3 5 b7 for m7, 1 3 5 b7 for the dominant 7, 1 3 5 7 for maj7 and 1 b3 b5 b7 for m7b5. The arpeggio is the skeleton of a line; scale notes, chromatics and passing notes go around it.

target-chord-tones.name: How to Target Chord Tones
target-chord-tones.theory: “Following the changes” starts with landing on a chord tone exactly when the chord changes. Over Am–C–Em–D work through four levels: roots first, then thirds (C, E, G, F#), fifths (E, G, B, A) and sevenths. The third tells you whether the chord is major or minor, the fifth sounds stable, the seventh adds colour. Start the line on the previous chord and finish it on the new one — that is what makes an improvisation audibly follow the harmony.

voice-leading.name: Voice Leading
voice-leading.theory: Voice leading means moving between chords by the shortest path: through a common tone or by a half or whole step. Gm and Bbm share Bb, and the D of Gm falls a half step to the Db of Bbm — the move shown in the video. Gm and Cm share G. Play that note right before the change and the line glides into the new chord instead of jumping. In a ii–V–I (Dm7–G7–Cmaj7) the shortest path runs through the thirds and sevenths: F→F→E and C→B→B.

switching-keys.name: How to Switch Keys While Improvising
switching-keys.term: How to Switch Keys While Improvising
switching-keys.theory: When a tune changes key, your scales and arpeggios have to change with it. A chord shared by both keys (pivot chord) or a ii–V that introduces the new key helps. Start with the easy move from C to F major, where only one note differs (B becomes Bb), then move on to G to B major. Work in this order: hear the change, pick the shape in the new key, then connect both keys with one line.

tritone-subs.name: Tritone Substitutions
tritone-subs.theory: A tritone substitution replaces a dominant chord with the dominant a tritone away: G7 → Db7. Both chords share the same tritone (B and F in G7, F and Cb = B in Db7), so they lead to the same chord, but the bass now moves chromatically: Dm7–Db7–Cmaj7 instead of Dm7–G7–Cmaj7. Over Db7 emphasize the third and seventh and resolve them by half step. The video shows the mechanism in Bm7–Bb7–Am7–Ab7–Gmaj7.

secondary-dominants.name: Secondary Dominants
secondary-dominants.theory: A secondary dominant is a dominant chord (V7) that briefly treats another chord of the key as its tonic. In C major: A7 leads to Dm7 (V7/ii), B7 to Em7, C7 to Fmaj7, D7 to G7, E7 to Am7; the video’s table adds G7 → Cmaj7, the regular dominant. Secondary dominants add tension and motion without changing the key. In Cmaj7–A7–Dm7–G7 each dominant leads to the next chord, and you hear it most clearly when you land on the target chord’s third.

borrowed-chords.name: Borrowed Chords
borrowed-chords.theory: Borrowed chords come from the parallel minor key. In C major you borrow them from C minor: Fm (iv), Bb7 (bVII7), Ab (bVI) and Eb (bIII). The best-known case is the backdoor ii–V: Fm7–Bb7–Cmaj7. Over Fm7 play F dorian, over Bb7 play Bb Lydian dominant or Bb mixolydian. The Bb bass rises a whole step into C, and that move is the “back door” sound.

melodic-minor.name: Melodic Minor Scale and Modes
melodic-minor.theory: The melodic minor scale (1 2 b3 4 5 6 7) is a minor scale with a major sixth and seventh: minor at the bottom, major on top. For improvisation it is more useful than harmonic minor, because its modes supply the scales for m(maj7), 7alt, 7#11 and other typical jazz sounds. Start with the A melodic minor box around fret 4, then play the next position up, and move both shapes to other keys with the selector.

chord-scale-melodic.name: Melodic Minor Chord/Scale Relationships
chord-scale-melodic.theory: Each mode of melodic minor fits a different chord: I melodic minor → m(maj7), II Dorian b2 → m7 (sus b9), III Lydian augmented → maj7#5, IV Lydian dominant → 7#11, V Mixolydian b6 → 7b13, VI Aeolian b5 (Locrian ♮2) → m7b5, VII Altered → 7alt. The video also pairs Altered with m7b5; usually, though, it is played over 7alt. When you see a chord symbol, you know which melodic minor to take the scale from: over G7alt you play Ab melodic minor.

harmonic-minor.name: Harmonic Minor Scale and Modes
harmonic-minor.theory: The harmonic minor scale (1 2 b3 4 5 b6 7) has a characteristic step and a half between b6 and 7 that gives it its “exotic” sound. It sits near the end of the learning order not because it is hard, but because it matters less for improvisation than everything before it. It is used most over the dominant of a minor key (E7 in A minor), where it brings out G#. Learn the C harmonic minor box around fret 6, then the next position up, and move both shapes to other keys.

chord-scale-harmonic.name: Harmonic Minor Chord/Scale Relationships
chord-scale-harmonic.theory: The modes of harmonic minor and their chords: I harmonic minor → m(maj7), II Locrian #6 → m7b5, III Ionian #5 → maj7#5, IV Dorian #4 → m7, V Phrygian dominant → 7, VI Lydian #2 → maj7, VII Superlocrian bb7 → dim7. In practice you will reach for Phrygian dominant most: over a V7 leading to a minor chord (E7 → Am) it brings b9 and b13, which pull towards the resolution. The other modes come up less often, but it pays to recognize their chord symbols.

giant-steps.name: Giant Steps
giant-steps.theory: John Coltrane’s “Giant Steps” closes the list. The key moves down by major thirds (B → G → Eb), often with a new chord every two beats. Each new key is introduced by its dominant (D7 → G, Bb7 → Eb, F#7 → B) or by a ii–V (Am7–D7, Fm7–Bb7, C#m7–F#7). Practice the whole 16-bar form in three steps: roots only, then a 1-2-3-5 pattern on each chord, finally arpeggios. Start at 60 BPM; once you get through the form without getting lost, all the earlier modules come together into one system.

blues-form.name: The 12-bar form
blues-form.theory: A blues is twelve bars and three chords: the I, IV and V of the key, all played as dominant chords (in A: A7, D7, E7). The layout is fixed: four bars of I, two of IV, two of I, then V, IV and two more bars of I. The quick change goes to IV in the second bar and comes back to I in the third. Before you solo, learn to hear which bar you are in: the move to IV in bar 5 and to V in bar 9 are the points every phrase leads to. Count the choruses out loud until you no longer need to.

blues-shuffle.name: Shuffle
blues-shuffle.theory: Eighth notes in the blues are not even: the first of each pair lasts two thirds of the beat, the second one third. It is a triplet rhythm with the middle note left out, and it is what makes the music swing. The basic accompaniment is the boogie riff: the root of the chord played with its fifth, then with its sixth, two eighths on each. Mute the strings with the heel of your picking hand right at the bridge so the riff sounds short and tight. The same shape moves to the IV and V chords.

blues-dominant-chords.name: Dominant chords
blues-dominant-chords.theory: A dominant chord is a major triad with a minor seventh added: 1, 3, 5, b7 (A7 = A, C#, E, G). In the blues all three chords are built this way, although in tonal music only the V would be a dominant. The third and the seventh form a tritone and give the chord its character; the root and the fifth matter less. That is why in a band the third and seventh alone, played on the D and G strings, are often enough. Play the arpeggios of the three chords to see where their thirds and sevenths sit.

blues-pentatonic.name: Pentatonic and the blues scale
blues-pentatonic.theory: The minor pentatonic (1 b3 4 5 b7) fits the whole blues form even though the chords are major. Its minor third rubs against the chord's major third, and that rub is what we hear as the blues sound. The blues scale adds one note: the b5, the so-called blue note, between the fourth and the fifth. Treat it as a passing note: move through it, do not stop on it. Stay in the first box for now; what you do with the notes matters more than how many you have.

blues-bends.name: Bends
blues-bends.theory: A bend changes the pitch smoothly, the way a voice does. Three bends are enough to start with: the fourth up to the fifth (a whole step on the G string), the minor seventh up to the root (a whole step on the B string) and the fourth up to the blue note (a half step). Bend with your third finger and put the first and second behind it on the same string to help; the movement comes from turning the wrist, not from the fingers alone. A separate gesture is the slight quarter-tone bend of the minor third towards the major third. Before you bend, play the target note normally and remember it: the bend has to land on that pitch, not near it.

blues-licks.name: A vocabulary of licks
blues-licks.theory: Blues improvisation is made largely of ready phrases, the way speech is made of words. Sing each lick first, then play it slowly, and only then at tempo. Once it sits under your fingers, change one thing about it: the rhythm, the last note, or where in the bar it starts. In the loop the lick is the question and your own phrase is the answer. Six licks played with confidence are worth more than sixty played without it.

blues-phrasing.name: Phrasing
blues-phrasing.theory: A blues solo is a conversation, not a stream of notes. Its oldest form is AAB, taken from blues lyrics: a phrase, the same phrase again over a different chord, and an answer. Each phrase takes about two bars and the next two are left for a breath. A rest is not a gap in the music: it is where the listener hears what you played. A good exercise is to play a whole chorus with one rhythmic motif and change only the notes.

blues-major-minor.name: Major and minor
blues-major-minor.theory: The major pentatonic (1 2 3 5 6) also fits over the I chord: it sounds brighter because it contains the chord's major third. Its box is the same shape as the minor pentatonic, three frets lower. The simplest rule for mixing them: major pentatonic over the I chord, minor over IV and V. Over the IV chord the key's major third clashes with that chord's seventh, so go back to the minor there. When both scales sit under your fingers in one place on the neck, you start playing one eight-note scale and choosing the colour note by note.

blues-boxes.name: Boxes on the top strings
blues-boxes.theory: Many blues guitarists play most of their solos on the top three strings, in small areas around the root. The best known sits around the root on the B string under the first finger: the second, fourth, fifth and sixth are within reach, and the second is bent up to the minor or major third. Another area is the top of the second pentatonic box, two frets above the first box; there the fourth and the seventh are the notes to bend. The areas are joined by a slide along one string. Change area with the phrase, not in the middle of it.

blues-turnarounds.name: Turnarounds
blues-turnarounds.theory: The last two bars of the form are the turnaround: a short figure that closes the chorus and leads into the next one. Harmonically it is usually I–IV–I–V, half a bar per chord, with the V chord at the very end. Melodically it is most often a chromatic line that walks down or up into a note of the V chord. The same figure works as an intro: played alone before bar one, it gives the band the key and the tempo. As an ending it stops on the I chord instead of the V.

blues-chord-tones.name: Chord tones
blues-chord-tones.theory: The pentatonic fits the whole form, but it does not say which chord is sounding. A chord tone played on beat one of the bar where the chord changes does. Start with the roots, then aim for the thirds: C# over A7, F# over D7, G# over E7. The thirds of these chords are not in the A minor pentatonic, so they are the notes that show the change most clearly. The rest of the phrase can stay in the pentatonic; it only has to land in the right place.

blues-guide-tones.name: Thirds and sevenths
blues-guide-tones.theory: The third and the seventh are the guide tones of a dominant chord. When the I chord changes to the IV they move by just a half step: the third of A7 (C#) falls to the seventh of D7 (C), and the seventh of A7 (G) falls to the third of D7 (F#). A line built from guide tones alone sounds as if it were playing the harmony. The full scale of each chord is the Mixolydian mode from its root (1 2 3 4 5 6 b7). In practice it is mixed with the minor pentatonic of the key.

blues-forms.name: Forms of the blues
blues-forms.theory: The twelve bars come in many versions. The quick change goes to IV in the second bar. A slow blues is played in 12/8 at a slow tempo, with room for long notes and bends. A minor blues turns the chords minor and often puts a bVI chord in bar 9 before the dominant. There are eight-bar and sixteen-bar forms too; in all of them the move to IV and the return to I remain the landmarks.

blues-jazz-blues.name: Jazz blues
blues-jazz-blues.theory: A jazz blues keeps the twelve bars and adds passing chords. Bar 4 brings a ii–V leading to the IV chord, bar 6 a diminished chord a half step above the IV, and bar 8 a dominant leading to the ii–V in bars 9–10. The form ends with a I–VI–ii–V turnaround. The blues scale of the key still holds everything together, but over the passing chords you need to aim for their thirds. Start with the arpeggios at a slow tempo.

triad-types.name: The four triad qualities
triad-types.theory: A triad is three notes stacked in thirds: the root, the third and the fifth. Its quality depends on the two thirds: major then minor gives a major chord, minor then major a minor one, two minor thirds a diminished one, two major thirds an augmented one. Major and minor have a perfect fifth, diminished a diminished fifth, augmented an augmented fifth. Every bigger chord, from sevenths to jazz extensions, has one of these four triads inside. That is why they are worth knowing by heart before you look for them on the neck.

triad-inversions.name: Inversions
triad-inversions.theory: The same three notes can be stacked three ways, depending on which one is lowest. Root position has the root in the bass (C E G), the first inversion the third (E G C), the second inversion the fifth (G C E). On three adjacent strings each inversion has its own shape, and all three follow each other up the neck and repeat every twelve frets. The highest note of an inversion is heard as the melody, so choosing an inversion changes how the chord sounds even though it is the same chord.

triad-diatonic.name: Triads in a key
triad-diatonic.theory: Building a triad on every degree of the major scale gives the seven chords of the key: I, IV and V are major, ii, iii and vi minor, and vii° diminished. In C major they are C, Dm, Em, F, G, Am and B°. On one string set these chords walk up the neck like a scale: every voice moves up by one scale note. This exercise ties what you know about keys to your hand and prepares you for voice leading.

triads-top.name: Strings 1-2-3
triads-top.theory: The three highest strings (G, B, E) are the most important set: triads sound clear above the bass here and stay out of the band's way. A major triad has three shapes that go up the neck in a fixed order, and the minor triad differs from each of them by one note: the third, one fret lower. Start with C major and C minor, learning where the root sits in every shape. Then play a progression with triads only, changing inversions so that your hand hardly moves.

triads-middle.name: Strings 2-3-4
triads-middle.theory: On the D, G and B strings the shapes differ from those above, because the G and B strings are a major third apart instead of a fourth. This set sounds fuller and darker and works well for comping with a bass player. Root position, first and second inversion again follow each other up the neck. Learn them on G major and G minor and compare them with the shapes on strings 1-2-3.

triads-low.name: Lower strings
triads-low.theory: On A, D, G and on E, A, D every pair of strings is a fourth apart, so the shapes are regular and easy to move. Triads sound dense and low here, so a band uses them less often, but in solo playing and riffs they are very useful. It is enough to master one of the two sets; the other differs only in where it sits on the neck. Practise on D major and D minor.

triads-caged.name: Triads in CAGED shapes
triads-caged.theory: Every barre chord and every open chord is made of triads on adjacent strings. The five CAGED shapes are five places on the neck where the same chord lies under the hand; in each of them you will find a triad on every string set. Once you see this, you can play a whole progression in one position, taking only three strings from each shape. The embedded visualizer shows the five shapes; compare them with the voicings in the exercise.

vl-common-tones.name: Common tones
vl-common-tones.theory: Voice leading means joining chords so that every note goes to the nearest note of the next chord. First rule: a note the two chords share stays where it is. Second: the other voices move by step, a half or a whole step. C and F share C, so when C changes to F, C stays, E goes to F and G to A. The hand hardly moves, and the chords sound like three smooth melodies instead of jumps.

vl-progressions.name: Progressions by the shortest way
vl-progressions.theory: The same rules apply to whole progressions. In I–V–vi–IV, ii–V–I or the Andalusian cadence (Am–G–F–E) every next triad lies a fret or two from the previous one. The top voice of these voicings forms a melody of its own; sing it while you play the chords. In the loop the microphone checks that you play the top voice of the right voicing on beat one of each chord.

vl-cycles.name: The cycle of fourths
vl-cycles.theory: The cycle of fourths goes through all twelve keys: C, F, Bb, Eb and on to G and back to C. Every two neighbouring chords share one note, and the other two voices move by a half or a whole step. This kind of drill comes from Mick Goodrick and is the fastest way to know triads in every key. Voice-led this way, the chords climb an octave over the whole cycle, so once along the way you have to jump down.

triad-melody.name: Triads in the solo
triad-melody.theory: A triad played note by note is the shortest way to a melody that sounds like the chord beneath it. Over each chord play only its three notes, and at the change move to the nearest note of the new triad. It is the same rule as voice leading, in a single line. Once that works, add scale notes in between, but land on triad notes.

triad-pairs.name: Triad pairs
triad-pairs.theory: A triad pair is two chords with no notes in common, played in turn, usually a whole step apart. Over Am7, F and G fit, the IV and V of C major: together they give six notes (F A C G B D) that sound modern and very sure of themselves. The method comes from jazz, where Gary Campbell among others described it. Play one triad up and the other down first, then mix them in short groups.

seventh-types.name: Seventh chord qualities
seventh-types.theory: A seventh chord is a triad with a seventh added: four notes stacked in thirds. Five qualities cover almost all music: maj7 (major triad and major seventh), 7 (major and minor seventh), m7 (minor and minor seventh), m7b5 (diminished and minor seventh) and dim7 (diminished and diminished seventh). The third and the seventh matter most: they say whether the chord is major or minor and what job it does. The root and fifth matter less, which is why guitarists often leave them out.

seventh-diatonic.name: Seventh chords in a key
seventh-diatonic.theory: Adding a seventh to every triad of a major key gives seven seventh chords: Imaj7, iim7, iiim7, IVmaj7, V7, vim7 and viim7b5. In C major they are Cmaj7, Dm7, Em7, Fmaj7, G7, Am7 and Bm7b5. Only one of them is a dominant (V7), and it pulls hardest towards the tonic. The ii–V–I, the most common move in jazz, is built on this set.

shells-sixth.name: Shell voicings: root on string 6
shells-sixth.theory: A shell voicing is a three-note chord: the root in the bass with the third and the seventh above it, no fifth. With the root on string 6 there are two layouts: root–seventh–third on strings 6, 4 and 3, and root–third–seventh on strings 6, 5 and 4. Changing the chord quality means moving one finger one fret: from maj7 to 7 the seventh drops, from 7 to m7 the third drops. Freddie Green used chords like these in the Count Basie band, playing four even strokes to the bar.

shells-fifth.name: Shell voicings: root on string 5
shells-fifth.theory: The same two layouts work with the root on string 5: root–seventh–third on strings 5, 3 and 2, and root–third–seventh on strings 5, 4 and 3. The shapes differ from the root-on-6 ones because the G and B strings are a major third apart instead of a fourth. Knowing both bass strings lets you play a whole progression in one place on the neck. Learn them from C and compare with the root-on-6 shapes.

shells-251.name: ii–V–I with shells
shells-251.theory: In a ii–V–I the roots leap a fourth, but the hand does not have to: ii with the root on string 5, V with the root on string 6, I back on string 5. The seventh of ii stays and becomes the third of V, and the seventh of V falls a half step to the third of I. The board in the exercise shows the nearest voicing, also when the bass string changes. Play four even strokes to the bar, short and light.

drop2-top.name: Drop 2 on strings 1-4
drop2-top.theory: A seventh chord in close position is hard to grab on the guitar. Drop 2 takes the second note from the top down an octave, so the four notes sit on four adjacent strings. Each of the four inversions has its own shape, and together they cover the whole neck. On strings 1-4 these voicings sound bright and are the ones most used for comping and chord melody.

drop2-middle.name: Drop 2 on strings 2-5
drop2-middle.theory: The same four inversions on the A, D, G and B strings sound fuller and lower. The shapes differ from strings 1-4 by moving the notes on the B string one fret. This set works well without a bass player or when the melody sits higher. Learn it from G and compare it with the voicings on strings 1-4.

drop2-251.name: ii–V–I with drop 2
drop2-251.theory: Joined by the shortest way, drop 2 voicings in a ii–V–I hardly move: every voice goes two frets at most, and some stay put. The top voice forms a melodic line of its own that is heard above the band. In the loop the microphone checks that you play the top voice on beat one of each chord. Once that works, try the progression in other keys with the selector.

drop3.name: Drop 3
drop3.theory: Drop 3 takes the third note from the top down an octave, which leaves a one-string gap between the bass and the rest of the chord. The voicings sit on strings 6-4-3-2 or 5-3-2-1, with the string in the gap muted by a finger. They sound wide, with a clear bass, and make a fuller replacement for shell voicings. They are harder to grab than drop 2, so play them slowly.

guide-tones.name: Guide tones
guide-tones.theory: The third and the seventh are enough to hear a chord. On the D and G strings they form a two-note shape that, in a ii–V–I and a jazz blues, moves from chord to chord by a half step or stays put. The third of one chord becomes the seventh of the next and the other way round. It is the lightest comping, leaving room for the bass and the soloists, and the best map of the harmony for improvising.

comping-rhythm.name: Comping rhythms
comping-rhythm.theory: Comping is rhythm first. In swing the simplest style is Freddie Green's: four short, even strokes to the bar, lightly accented on 2 and 4. The Charleston is a stroke on beat one and on the and of beat two. In bossa nova the chords fall on a fixed syncopated pattern locked with the drums. Settle the rhythm first and only then add voicings.

comping-standards.name: Comping standards
comping-standards.theory: Finally everything together: real standard progressions, drop 2 voicings by the shortest way and a swing feel. Autumn Leaves is a chain of ii–V–Is in major and minor, Rhythm changes moves a chord every two beats, and All the Things You Are travels between distant keys. Pick one progression, slow it down and play until you stop thinking about the shapes.

ear-tonic.name: Tonic, third and fifth
ear-tonic.theory: Functional ear training starts from the key, not from single notes. A I–IV–V–I cadence sets the tonic in your head, and every note after it sounds like one of its degrees: the tonic like coming home, the third bright and calm, the fifth open, as if something else were coming. You start with just these three degrees, because they form the tonic chord. When unsure, sing in your head from the note you heard down to the tonic; the number of steps gives the degree. The key changes with every question, so you learn relationships, not pitches.

ear-degrees.name: All major degrees
ear-degrees.theory: The other degrees tell you where they want to go. The seventh pulls a half step up to the tonic, the fourth down to the third, the second to the tonic or the third, the sixth to the fifth. That pull is the surest clue: after hearing a note, feel where it would like to resolve. The Benbassat and Arnold method is simple: a cadence, one note, an answer, hundreds of times, in ever-changing keys.

ear-minor.name: Minor degrees
ear-minor.theory: Minor has the same tonic and fifth, but the third, sixth and seventh sit a half step lower (b3, b6, b7). An i–iv–V–i cadence with a major dominant tells you at once that you are in minor. The b3 sounds darker than the major third, the b6 pulls down to the fifth, and the b7 no longer leads so strongly to the tonic. The answers name the degrees against major, the way jazz and rock players describe them.

ear-intervals-up.name: Ascending intervals: the easy ones
ear-intervals-up.theory: An interval is the distance between two notes, with no key. Start with the five most distinct: minor and major third, fourth, fifth and octave. A minor third sounds sad, a major third bright, a fourth like a call, a fifth empty and strong, an octave like the same note higher. Openings of well-known tunes help too, but the character of the interval is more reliable. On the fretboard these are the commonest shapes: a fourth is the same fret on the next higher string (except the G–B pair).

ear-intervals-all.name: All intervals, up and down
ear-intervals-all.theory: Now the full set from the minor second to the octave, also descending. Seconds sound like a scale step, the major sixth like a wide, bright leap, the minor seventh like a dominant chord without its middle, the tritone unstable. Descending intervals are harder, because the ear wants to hear the last note as the tonic; singing both notes from the bottom up helps. The extra exercise ties this to the fretboard: hear two notes and play them.

ear-intervals-harmonic.name: Intervals played together
ear-intervals-harmonic.theory: When two notes sound at once, there is no direction, only the colour of the sound. Thirds and sixths sound soft and full, fourths, fifths and octaves empty, and seconds, sevenths and the tritone rough. This is the basis of double stops and of the guide tones in seventh chords. If you cannot name an interval, pick out the lower note in your head, then the upper one, and turn it into a melodic interval.

ear-triads.name: Major, minor, diminished, augmented
ear-triads.theory: The four triad qualities differ in their third and fifth. Major sounds bright and stable, minor darker, diminished tense and tight (two minor thirds), augmented uncertain and blurred (two major thirds). The quiz plays real guitar voicings on different strings and in different inversions, so you listen for the quality, not for one shape. After the strum, the chord is also played note by note.

ear-sevenths.name: Seventh chords
ear-sevenths.theory: maj7 sounds soft and dreamy, because the major seventh sits a half step below the octave. 7 (dominant) has a tritone between its third and seventh and wants to resolve. m7 sounds mellow and warm, m7b5 dark and restless. The quiz plays the drop 2 voicings of the Seventh chords track.

ear-inversions.name: What is in the bass
ear-inversions.theory: The same chord sounds different depending on its lowest note. The root in the bass gives the fullest, most stable sound. The third in the bass is lighter and seems to move, which is why it shows up in passing bass lines. The fifth in the bass sounds suspended and usually leads on. Listen to the lowest note on its own: sing it in your head and check whether it is the chord's root.

ear-functions.name: Chord function
ear-functions.theory: After a cadence, every chord of the key has its role. I is home, IV moves away with a bright sound, V comes back with tension, vi is the tonic's minor relative, ii is the minor chord before V, and iii, the rarest, sounds soft and minor. Listen to the bass, which points to the degree, while the chord quality (major or minor) narrows the choice. Upper case marks major chords, lower case minor ones.

ear-progressions.name: Four-chord progressions
ear-progressions.theory: Most songs use a handful of the same progressions: I–V–vi–IV, I–vi–IV–V, I–IV–V–I, ii–V–I. Follow the bass line chord by chord and name the degrees in your head. It helps to catch the minor chords (ii, iii, vi) and the spot where the tonic returns. This is the skill that lets you play a song by ear without looking up the chords.

ear-echo.name: Play what you hear
ear-echo.theory: The last step ties your ear to the fretboard. The app plays a cadence and a short phrase, and you play it back on the guitar in any octave; the microphone checks it note by note. Find the tonic on the fretboard first, then think in degrees. Phrases start with three notes within the first five degrees, then four notes from the whole scale. Sing the phrase before you play it: what you can sing, you will easily find on the fretboard. Play with headphones if you can, so the microphone does not hear the speaker.

pentatonic-scale.licks.name: Licks in box 1
pentatonic-scale.licks.desc: Three short phrases from the first pentatonic box. Listen, play them a few times, then use them over the loop.

pentatonic-positions.licks.name: Licks across boxes
pentatonic-positions.licks.desc: Two phrases that move from box to box and along one string.

arpeggios.licks.name: Arpeggio licks
arpeggios.licks.desc: Phrases built from chord tones only, including a whole ii–V–I.

target-chord-tones.licks.name: Licks landing on the third
target-chord-tones.licks.desc: Two pentatonic phrases that end on the third of the chord.

pentatonic-scale.e9.name: Loop: licks in their bars
pentatonic-scale.e9.desc: The prompter says in which bar to play a lick and in which to answer your own way.

target-chord-tones.e6.name: Loop: licks on the third
target-chord-tones.e6.desc: Two licks from this module in their bars, then two bars for your own landings.

standards.e1.name: Loop: progressions from standards
standards.e1.desc: Progressions from the real repertoire. Pick one, slow the tempo down and play what the modules taught you. This section blocks nothing.

e-string-notes.e1.name: Practice: position → note (E string)
e-string-notes.e1.desc: Open the “fretboard → note” practice on the E string, frets 1–12. Every position needs at least 3 answers and 80% accuracy.

e-string-notes.e2.name: Practice: note → position (E string)
e-string-notes.e2.desc: The reverse direction: read a note name and point to it in the tab. It uses the same position stats as the previous exercise. Extra practice — not required to pass the module.

key-signatures.e1.name: Quiz: notes of the key
key-signatures.e1.desc: Which notes make up a key and which of them are raised or lowered. The key is marked on the circle of fifths, and after you answer the circle shows its chords.

key-signatures.e2.name: Note in the key
key-signatures.e2.desc: The decision you make in a solo: you play in the given key and pick the note that belongs to it, for example G or G#.

pentatonic-scale.e1.name: Diagram: minor pentatonic, box 1
pentatonic-scale.e1.desc: Box 1 of the minor pentatonic (A minor by default, frets 5–8). The selector changes the key and the shape slides along the neck. A run is the whole scale up and down. The colours show how the box is built: a rectangle (two strings, notes 3 frets apart) and a stack (three strings, 2 frets apart). The “View” switch adds the blue note, the second, or marks the notes to bend.

pentatonic-scale.e2.name: Diagram: minor pentatonic, box 2
pentatonic-scale.e2.desc: Box 2, starting on the minor third (frets 7–10 in A minor). It connects to box 1 and extends the scale up the neck.

major-scale.e1.name: Diagram: major scale, lower position
major-scale.e1.desc: The major scale in one position (A major, frets 2–6). Use the selector to move it to other keys.

major-scale.e2.name: Diagram: major scale, higher position
major-scale.e2.desc: The same scale in the next position (C major, frets 7–11).

fretboard-notes.e1.name: Practice: position → note (whole neck)
fretboard-notes.e1.desc: Open the “fretboard → note” practice on all strings, frets 1–12. Every position needs at least 3 answers and 80% accuracy.

fretboard-notes.e2.name: Practice: note → position (whole neck)
fretboard-notes.e2.desc: The reverse direction across the neck. It uses the same position stats as the previous exercise. Extra practice — not required to pass the module.

pentatonic-positions.e1.name: Box 1: from G (fret 3)
pentatonic-positions.e1.desc: Box 1 of G minor pentatonic, frets 3–6.

pentatonic-positions.e2.name: Box 2: from Bb (fret 5)
pentatonic-positions.e2.desc: Box 2 of the same scale, starting on Bb — “Bb major pent” in the video. Frets 5–8.

pentatonic-positions.e3.name: Box 3: from C (fret 7)
pentatonic-positions.e3.desc: Box 3, starting on C — “C dorian pent” in the video. Frets 7–11.

pentatonic-positions.e4.name: Box 4: from D (fret 10)
pentatonic-positions.e4.desc: Box 4, starting on D — “D phrygian pent” in the video. Frets 10–13.

pentatonic-positions.e5.name: Box 5: from F (fret 12)
pentatonic-positions.e5.desc: Box 5, starting on F — “F mixolydian pent” in the video. Frets 12–15.

modes.e1.name: Quiz: modes
modes.e1.desc: The characteristic note of a mode on the fretboard, a mode's notes from a given root, the parent scale on the circle, and recognizing modes by ear.

modes.e2.name: Characteristic note on the fretboard
modes.e2.desc: Find the note that gives a mode its sound: 6 in Dorian, #4 in Lydian, b7 in Mixolydian.

chord-construction.e1.name: Quiz: chords from the scale
chord-construction.e1.desc: Build a chord on a degree of the major scale: tap its notes on the fretboard and name its type — triads and seventh chords.

chord-construction.e2.name: Build the chord on the fretboard
chord-construction.e2.desc: The chord's root is highlighted. Tap its third, fifth or seventh — every other note of the scale.

chord-scale-major.e1.name: Chord → mode (major)
chord-scale-major.e1.desc: Dm7 → Dorian, Fmaj7 → Lydian, G7 → Mixolydian…

chord-scale-major.e2.name: Characteristic note over the chord
chord-scale-major.e2.desc: For a chord in a key, tap the characteristic note of the matching mode — the one worth resting a phrase on.

triads.e1.name: Loop: triads over Am–C–Em–D
triads.e1.desc: Play only triads over the loop, moving each inversion by the smallest finger movement. 2 successful loops.

triads.e2.name: Name → intervals
triads.e2.desc: Major 1 3 5, minor 1 b3 5, dim, aug + seventh chords.

arpeggios.e1.name: Diagram: m7 arpeggio
arpeggios.e1.desc: Cm7 arpeggio (1 b3 5 b7) across all strings, frets 8–12.

arpeggios.e2.name: Diagram: 7 (dominant) arpeggio
arpeggios.e2.desc: G7 arpeggio (1 3 5 b7) across all strings, frets 3–7.

target-chord-tones.e1.name: Loop: roots, thirds, fifths, sevenths
target-chord-tones.e1.desc: Am–C–Em–D in four levels. Land on the given chord tone at every change; each level needs its own successful loops.

target-chord-tones.e2.name: Loop: any chord tone
target-chord-tones.e2.desc: The same progression with no fixed target — land on any chord tone.

voice-leading.e1.name: Loop: Gm → Bbm
voice-leading.e1.desc: Before the change play the common tone (Bb) or a neighbouring step.

voice-leading.e2.name: Loop: Gm → Cm
voice-leading.e2.desc: Common tone: G. Minimize finger movement.

switching-keys.e1.name: Quiz: common chords and ii–V
switching-keys.e1.desc: Pivot chords between keys and the ii–V that announces a key.

switching-keys.e2.name: Loop: C major → F major
switching-keys.e2.desc: The easier change — one note differs (B becomes Bb).

tritone-subs.e1.name: Quiz: tritone substitutions
tritone-subs.e1.desc: subV for G7? V for a subV? subV→I resolution.

tritone-subs.e2.name: Loop: G7 and Db7
tritone-subs.e2.desc: Three variants: a plain ii–V–I, the same progression with Db7 and the video’s chain. Each variant needs its own successful loops.

secondary-dominants.e1.name: Quiz: secondary dominants
secondary-dominants.e1.desc: Find the secondary dominant of a chord in the key and the chord it leads to — in every major key.

secondary-dominants.e2.name: Loop: secondary dominants
secondary-dominants.e2.desc: Two variants: Cmaj7–A7–Dm7–G7 and a progression with five dominants. After each dominant, land on the third of the next chord.

borrowed-chords.e1.name: Quiz: borrowed chords
borrowed-chords.e1.desc: Name the degree of a chord borrowed from the parallel minor and recognize the backdoor progression.

borrowed-chords.e2.name: Loop: ii–V–I and backdoor
borrowed-chords.e2.desc: Two variants leading to Cmaj7: Dm7–G7 and Fm7–Bb7. Compare how they sound.

melodic-minor.e1.name: Diagram: A melodic minor, lower position
melodic-minor.e1.desc: The scale 1 2 b3 4 5 6 7 at frets 3–7. Use the selector to move it to other keys.

melodic-minor.e2.name: Diagram: A melodic minor, higher position
melodic-minor.e2.desc: The next position of the same scale, frets 7–11.

chord-scale-melodic.e1.name: Quiz: melodic minor modes
chord-scale-melodic.e1.desc: Chord → mode, mode → chord and the parent scale of a specific chord.

chord-scale-melodic.e2.name: Quiz: which melodic minor?
chord-scale-melodic.e2.desc: For a chord (e.g. D7#11), name the melodic minor its scale comes from.

harmonic-minor.e1.name: Diagram: C harmonic minor, lower position
harmonic-minor.e1.desc: The scale 1 2 b3 4 5 b6 7 at frets 5–9. Use the selector to move it to other keys.

harmonic-minor.e2.name: Diagram: C harmonic minor, higher position
harmonic-minor.e2.desc: The next position of the same scale, frets 10–14.

chord-scale-harmonic.e1.name: Quiz: harmonic minor modes
chord-scale-harmonic.e1.desc: Chord → mode, mode → chord and the parent scale of a specific chord.

chord-scale-harmonic.e2.name: Quiz: which harmonic minor?
chord-scale-harmonic.e2.desc: For a chord (e.g. E7), name the harmonic minor its scale comes from.

giant-steps.e1.name: Quiz: the Coltrane cycle
giant-steps.e1.desc: Key order, the dominants and ii–Vs leading to B, G and Eb, and the cycle moved to other keys.

giant-steps.e2.name: Loop: Giant Steps
giant-steps.e2.desc: The whole 16-bar form from 60 BPM, in three levels: roots, a 1-2-3-5 pattern, arpeggios. Each level needs a successful loop.

pentatonic-scale.e3.name: Practice: A minor pentatonic
pentatonic-scale.e3.desc: Play the A minor pentatonic notes (frets 5–8) in the practice session with live scoring. Extra practice session — not required to pass the module.

major-scale.e3.name: Practice: C major scale
major-scale.e3.desc: Play the C major scale notes (frets 8–12) in the practice session with live scoring. Extra practice session — not required to pass the module.

melodic-minor.e3.name: Practice: A melodic minor
melodic-minor.e3.desc: Play the A melodic minor notes (frets 5–9) in the practice session with live scoring. Extra practice session — not required to pass the module.

harmonic-minor.e3.name: Practice: C harmonic minor
harmonic-minor.e3.desc: Play the C harmonic minor notes (frets 5–9) in the practice session with live scoring. Extra practice session — not required to pass the module.

pentatonic-scale.e4.name: Loop: improvise in box 1
pentatonic-scale.e4.desc: Improvise over Am7 (four bars) – Dm7 – Em7 using only the first pentatonic box (frets 5–8). 2 successful loops.

major-scale.e4.name: Loop: C major phrases
major-scale.e4.desc: Phrase with the C major scale over Cmaj7–Am7–Fmaj7–G7 and end your lines on C. 2 successful loops.

pentatonic-positions.e9.name: Build the box from a root
pentatonic-positions.e9.desc: You get one root G and the finger that holds it. Tap the rest of the box — six starting positions rebuild all five boxes. Extra practice.

pentatonic-positions.e7.name: Diagram: moving diagonally
pentatonic-positions.e7.desc: Three neighbouring boxes at once. The highlighted stack repeats an octave higher, so the same lick takes you diagonally across the neck. Extra practice.

pentatonic-positions.e8.name: Diagram: the pentatonic on one string
pentatonic-positions.e8.desc: The whole G minor pentatonic on the G string, from the open string to fret 12. It teaches the distances between notes instead of a box shape. Extra practice.

pentatonic-positions.e6.name: Loop: box to box
pentatonic-positions.e6.desc: Gm7–Cm7: move to a neighbouring pentatonic box with each loop. 2 successful loops.

modes.e4.name: Diagram: pentatonic + 2 notes = mode
modes.e4.desc: Every mode is a pentatonic from the same root with two notes added. The minor one gives Dorian, Aeolian and Phrygian; the major one gives Lydian, Ionian and Mixolydian. Extra practice.

modes.e5.name: Loop: pentatonic, then the mode
modes.e5.desc: One Dm7 chord for eight bars: first the pentatonic alone, then Dorian. Extra practice.

pentatonic-scale.e7.name: Loop: constraints
pentatonic-scale.e7.desc: Extra practice. Three variants: three notes only, one string only, a set rhythm. Fewer notes to choose from, more attention on rhythm and phrasing.

pentatonic-scale.e8.name: Loop: blues, minor and major
pentatonic-scale.e8.desc: Extra practice. Blues in A three ways: minor pentatonic, major pentatonic, and both in turn.

pentatonic-positions.e10.name: Loop: blues in G, minor and major
pentatonic-positions.e10.desc: Extra practice. Blues in G: minor pentatonic, major pentatonic, and both in turn. Move between the boxes as you play.

target-chord-tones.e5.name: Loop: approach notes
target-chord-tones.e5.desc: Extra practice. Approach the chord's root from a half step below, then surround it from above and below. The microphone checks the landing on beat one.

voice-leading.e4.name: Loop: approaching the thirds
voice-leading.e4.desc: Extra practice. Dm7–G7–Cmaj7: reach the third of each chord chromatically. The microphone checks the third on beat one.

modes.e6.name: Loop: modes from one root
modes.e6.desc: Extra practice. A chord on D keeps playing while the variant changes the mode: Dorian, Aeolian, Phrygian, Mixolydian, Lydian.

modes.e3.name: Loop: modal colors
modes.e3.desc: Four variants (Dorian, Phrygian, Lydian, Mixolydian). Emphasize the mode's characteristic note over each backing. 2 successful loops per variant.

chord-scale-major.e3.name: Loop: characteristic tones
chord-scale-major.e3.desc: Dm7–G7–Cmaj7 with a scale hint on each chord. Play the chord's characteristic tone at every change. 2 successful loops.

arpeggios.e3.name: Loop: arpeggios over ii–V–I
arpeggios.e3.desc: Dm7–G7–Cmaj7: play only chord arpeggios — no scale notes. 2 successful loops.

voice-leading.e3.name: Loop: thirds and sevenths in ii–V–I
voice-leading.e3.desc: Dm7–G7–Cmaj7: lead the thirds and sevenths (F→F→E, C→B→B). The mic checks thirds and sevenths.

switching-keys.e3.name: Loop: G major → B major
switching-keys.e3.desc: Halfway through the loop the key jumps a major third — move your scales and arpeggios to the new key.

chord-scale-melodic.e3.name: Loop: minor ii–V–i
chord-scale-melodic.e3.desc: Dm7b5–G7alt–Cm(maj7) or a single D7#11 — a scale hint on every chord.

melodic-minor.e4.name: Loop: Am6 – Am(maj7)
melodic-minor.e4.desc: Two shades of A minor: emphasize the 6 (F#) and the major 7 (G#). 2 successful loops.

harmonic-minor.e4.name: Loop: Am – E7
harmonic-minor.e4.desc: Over E7 emphasize G# — the characteristic note of A harmonic minor. 2 successful loops.

chord-scale-harmonic.e3.name: Loop: minor ii–V with harmonic minor
chord-scale-harmonic.e3.desc: Bm7b5–E7–Am: use Phrygian dominant over E7. 2 successful loops.

pentatonic-scale.e5.name: Loop: 12-bar blues
pentatonic-scale.e5.desc: 12-bar blues in A (A7–D7–E7). Improvise in pentatonic box 1. 2 successful loops.

target-chord-tones.e3.name: Loop: 12-bar blues
target-chord-tones.e3.desc: 12-bar blues in A — land on a chord tone at every change. 2 successful loops.

arpeggios.e4.name: Diagram: maj7 arpeggio
arpeggios.e4.desc: Cmaj7 arpeggio (1 3 5 7) across all strings, frets 7–11 — the I chord of the ii–V–I loop.

arpeggios.e5.name: Diagram: m7b5 arpeggio
arpeggios.e5.desc: Bm7b5 arpeggio (1 b3 b5 b7) across all strings, frets 7–11 — the vii chord of C major and the ii of a minor ii–V.

pentatonic-scale.e6.name: Loop: phrase and rest
pentatonic-scale.e6.desc: Extra practice. Am7–Am7–Dm7–Em7 in box 1: play a bar and rest a bar, or a two-bar question and a two-bar answer.

target-chord-tones.e4.name: Loop: phrase and rest
target-chord-tones.e4.desc: Extra practice. Am–C–Em–D: play a bar and rest a bar, or a two-bar question and a two-bar answer; end each phrase on a chord tone.

blues-form.e1.name: Quiz: the 12-bar form
blues-form.e1.desc: Which chord sounds in which bar. Questions in several keys, including the quick change.

blues-form.e2.name: Quiz: I, IV and V in a key
blues-form.e2.desc: Find the three chords of a blues in the given key.

blues-form.e3.name: Loop: roots on beat one
blues-form.e3.desc: Blues in A. On the first beat of every bar play the root of the chord that is sounding. The microphone checks the hits.

blues-form.e4.name: Loop: roots with a quick change
blues-form.e4.desc: The same exercise, but the IV chord comes in bar 2.

blues-shuffle.licks.name: The boogie riff
blues-shuffle.licks.desc: Two accompaniment riffs: the root with the fifth and the sixth, and a version with the seventh. Listen for the long and short eighths.

blues-shuffle.e1.name: Loop: the riff through the form
blues-shuffle.e1.desc: Play the boogie riff for 12 bars, moving it to the IV and V chords. Mark the loop when you did not lose the form.

blues-dominant-chords.e1.name: Quiz: tones of dominant chords
blues-dominant-chords.e1.desc: Thirds and sevenths of the chords and how they move when the I changes to the IV.

blues-dominant-chords.e2.name: Diagram: A7, D7, E7 arpeggios
blues-dominant-chords.e2.desc: The "Shape" selector changes the chord. Play the arpeggio of each of the three chords up and down.

blues-dominant-chords.e3.name: Loop: comping
blues-dominant-chords.e3.desc: Play A7, D7 and E7 through the form: full shapes or just the thirds and sevenths.

blues-pentatonic.e1.name: Diagram: minor pentatonic, box 1
blues-pentatonic.e1.desc: The first box of the minor pentatonic. The "View" selector adds the blue note or marks the notes to bend.

blues-pentatonic.e2.name: Loop: your first solo
blues-pentatonic.e2.desc: Blues in A. Improvise in the first pentatonic box.

blues-pentatonic.e3.name: Loop: constraints
blues-pentatonic.e3.desc: The same blues with one constraint at a time: three notes, one string or one rhythm.

blues-pentatonic.e4.name: Practice: pentatonic notes
blues-pentatonic.e4.desc: Play the notes of A minor pentatonic on frets 5–8 in the microphone mode.

blues-bends.e1.name: Half-step bend
blues-bends.e1.desc: The fourth up to the blue note on the G string. The meter shows how far you are from the target.

blues-bends.e2.name: Whole-step bend
blues-bends.e2.desc: The two most important bends in the blues: the fourth to the fifth on the G string and the seventh to the root on the B string.

blues-bends.e3.name: Quarter-tone bend
blues-bends.e3.desc: The minor third nudged up towards the major third. The note should stay between the frets.

blues-bends.licks.name: Licks with a bend
blues-bends.licks.desc: Three short phrases in which the bend is the most important note.

blues-licks.licks.name: Six licks in box 1
blues-licks.licks.desc: A basic vocabulary: an opener, triplets, the blue note, a slide, an answer and a phrase on the bass strings.

blues-licks.e1.name: Loop: lick and answer
blues-licks.e1.desc: In bars 1, 5 and 9 play the named lick; in the others answer with your own phrase.

blues-phrasing.e1.name: Loop: the AAB form
blues-phrasing.e1.desc: A phrase, the phrase again and an answer, two bars each, with two bars of rest after each one.

blues-phrasing.e2.name: Loop: play a bar, rest a bar
blues-phrasing.e2.desc: Four bars with a cue for when to play and when to listen. The second variant is question and answer.

blues-phrasing.e3.name: Loop: one motif
blues-phrasing.e3.desc: A whole chorus with one rhythmic motif. Only the notes change.

blues-major-minor.e1.name: Diagram: major pentatonic
blues-major-minor.e1.desc: The major pentatonic box: the same shape as the minor one, three frets lower.

blues-major-minor.e2.name: Quiz: scales in the blues
blues-major-minor.e2.desc: The blue note, the notes of the major pentatonic and how it relates to the minor one.

blues-major-minor.e3.name: Loop: major, minor and both
blues-major-minor.e3.desc: Three variants of the same blues: minor pentatonic, major pentatonic, and changing colour with the chord.

blues-major-minor.e4.name: Diagram: both pentatonics together
blues-major-minor.e4.desc: The minor and major pentatonic from the same root in one place on the neck, and the major blues scale.

blues-boxes.e1.name: Diagram: the box around the root on the B string
blues-boxes.e1.desc: Five notes on the top three strings. The root is on the B string under the first finger.

blues-boxes.e2.name: Diagram: the top of box 2
blues-boxes.e2.desc: The second pentatonic box on the top three strings. The fourth and the seventh are bent a whole step here.

blues-boxes.e3.name: Loop: change area every 4 bars
blues-boxes.e3.desc: Bars 1–4 in box 1, bars 5–8 at the top of box 2, bars 9–12 around the root on the B string.

blues-boxes.e4.name: Diagram: the diagonal through the boxes
blues-boxes.e4.desc: The same three-string pattern repeats higher up the neck and joins the boxes into one line.

blues-boxes.licks.name: Licks around the root on the B string
blues-boxes.licks.desc: Two phrases that bend the second up to the third.

blues-turnarounds.licks.name: Two turnarounds
blues-turnarounds.licks.desc: A chromatic line down and one up. Both end on a note of the V chord.

blues-turnarounds.e1.name: Loop: turnaround in bars 11–12
blues-turnarounds.e1.desc: Improvise for 10 bars and close the last two with a turnaround.

blues-chord-tones.e1.name: Loop: the chord-tone ladder
blues-chord-tones.e1.desc: Three levels: on beat one of every bar land on the root, then on the third, then on the seventh of the chord.

blues-chord-tones.e2.name: Loop: approach from below
blues-chord-tones.e2.desc: Just before beat one play the note a half step below the chord's third and land on the third.

blues-guide-tones.e1.name: Diagram: the Mixolydian mode
blues-guide-tones.e1.desc: The scale of each of the three chords: A, D and E Mixolydian. The "Shape" selector changes the chord.

blues-guide-tones.e2.name: Quiz: how guide tones move
blues-guide-tones.e2.desc: Which note the third of the I chord falls to when the IV chord arrives.

blues-guide-tones.e3.name: Loop: thirds and sevenths
blues-guide-tones.e3.desc: On beat one of every bar play the third or the seventh of the chord. Look for half-step moves.

blues-forms.e1.name: Quiz: the quick change
blues-forms.e1.desc: Chords in the bars of the form with the early move to IV.

blues-forms.e2.name: Loop: five forms
blues-forms.e2.desc: Quick change, slow blues, minor blues, the eight-bar and the sixteen-bar form. Each one has to be played.

blues-jazz-blues.e1.name: Diagram: jazz blues arpeggios
blues-jazz-blues.e1.desc: F7, Gm7 and C7: the chords the form in F is built around.

blues-jazz-blues.e2.name: Loop: jazz blues in F
blues-jazz-blues.e2.desc: On every chord change land on the chord's third. Start at a slow tempo.

blues-jam.e1.name: Loop: blues jam
blues-jam.e1.desc: Every blues form in one place. Pick a form, a key and a style, then just play. This section gates nothing.

triad-types.e1.name: Quiz: triad qualities
triad-types.e1.desc: The intervals of each of the four triad qualities and what each is called.

triad-types.e2.name: Quiz: triad notes on the fretboard
triad-types.e2.desc: Find the third, fifth or seventh of a chord built on a degree of the key.

triad-inversions.e1.name: Quiz: inversions
triad-inversions.e1.desc: Tell the inversion from the bass note and build an inversion from the bottom.

triad-inversions.e2.name: Voicings: the three inversions of C major
triad-inversions.e2.desc: Root position, first and second inversion on strings 1-2-3, up the neck. One voicing per bar.

triad-inversions.e3.name: Voicings: the three inversions of A minor
triad-inversions.e3.desc: The same exercise with a minor triad.

triad-diatonic.e1.name: Quiz: triads in a key
triad-diatonic.e1.desc: Which triad sits on a given degree of a major key.

triad-diatonic.e2.name: Voicings: C major up the neck
triad-diatonic.e2.desc: C, Dm, Em, F, G, Am, B° and C on strings 1-2-3. Every voice moves up one scale note.

triad-diatonic.e3.name: Voicings: the key on strings 2-3-4
triad-diatonic.e3.desc: The same sequence on the middle strings.

triads-top.e1.name: Voicings: major and minor on strings 1-2-3
triads-top.e1.desc: Every voicing of C major and C minor across the neck. The "Chord" selector changes the quality.

triads-top.e2.name: Loop: comping with triads
triads-top.e2.desc: G–D–Em–C on strings 1-2-3. The board shows the voicing nearest to the previous one.

triads-top.e3.name: Voicings: diminished and augmented
triads-top.e3.desc: C° and C+ on strings 1-2-3. The augmented triad repeats every four frets.

triads-middle.e1.name: Voicings: major and minor on strings 2-3-4
triads-middle.e1.desc: Every voicing of G major and G minor across the neck.

triads-middle.e2.name: Loop: comping on the middle strings
triads-middle.e2.desc: G–D–Em–C on strings 2-3-4, each voicing nearest to the previous one.

triads-low.e1.name: Voicings: major and minor on the lower strings
triads-low.e1.desc: D major and D minor on strings 3-4-5 or 4-5-6. Pick the set with the selector.

triads-low.e2.name: Loop: comping on the lower strings

triads-low.e3.name: Voicings: diminished and augmented
triads-low.e3.desc: D° and D+ on the lower strings.

triads-caged.e1.name: Voicings: G major on four string sets
triads-caged.e1.desc: Go through the G major voicings on every string set. Four runs, ideally one per set.

triads-caged.e2.name: Loop: one position
triads-caged.e2.desc: G–C–D–G on strings 2-3-4 around frets 2–6. The whole progression without moving your hand.

vl-common-tones.e1.name: Quiz: voice leading
vl-common-tones.e1.desc: The notes two chords share and where each voice goes at the change.

vl-common-tones.e2.name: Voicings: C–F–G–C by the shortest way
vl-common-tones.e2.desc: Common notes are green, and arrows show where the other voices move.

vl-common-tones.e3.name: Voicings: Am–Dm–E–Am
vl-common-tones.e3.desc: The same rule in a minor key.

vl-progressions.e1.name: Loop: three progressions
vl-progressions.e1.desc: I–V–vi–IV, ii–V–I and the Andalusian cadence on strings 1-2-3. The microphone checks the top voice.

vl-progressions.e2.name: Loop: progressions on strings 2-3-4
vl-progressions.e2.desc: The same progressions on the middle strings.

vl-cycles.e1.name: Voicings: the cycle of fourths
vl-cycles.e1.desc: Twelve major triads in fourths, each voice-led from the previous one.

vl-cycles.e2.name: Loop: the cycle of fourths
vl-cycles.e2.desc: The whole cycle over a backing, one chord per bar. Start slowly.

vl-cycles.e3.name: Voicings: the cycle of fourths in minor

triad-melody.licks.name: Phrases from triads
triad-melody.licks.desc: A C major arpeggio and a phrase that follows the chords C–Am–F–G.

triad-melody.e1.name: Loop: triad notes only
triad-melody.e1.desc: Over each chord play only its three notes. The microphone checks beat one of every bar.

triad-melody.e2.name: Loop: the top-voice melody
triad-melody.e2.desc: Play only the top voice of the voicings as a melody.

triad-pairs.e1.name: Diagram: the triad-pair scale
triad-pairs.e1.desc: The six notes of the F and G triads over A minor in one position.

triad-pairs.e2.name: Loop: F and G over Am7
triad-pairs.e2.desc: Groups from the F triad and from the G triad in turn over one chord.

triad-pairs.licks.name: Phrases from a triad pair
triad-pairs.licks.desc: Two phrases from F and G over A minor: up through both triads and down.

seventh-types.e1.name: Quiz: chord intervals
seventh-types.e1.desc: The intervals of each chord quality, sevenths included, and what each is called.

seventh-types.e2.name: Quiz: the seventh of a dominant chord
seventh-types.e2.desc: Find the seventh of a 7 chord in different keys.

seventh-diatonic.e1.name: Quiz: seventh chords in a key
seventh-diatonic.e1.desc: Which seventh chord sits on a given degree of a major key.

seventh-diatonic.e2.name: Diagram: maj7, m7, 7 and m7b5 arpeggios
seventh-diatonic.e2.desc: Four chords of C major as arpeggios in one position. The "Shape" selector changes the chord.

shells-sixth.e1.name: Voicings: root–seventh–third
shells-sixth.e1.desc: Gmaj7, G7, Gm7 and Gm7b5 on strings 6, 4 and 3. The "Chord" selector changes the quality.

shells-sixth.e2.name: Voicings: root–third–seventh
shells-sixth.e2.desc: The same four chords on strings 6, 5 and 4.

shells-fifth.e1.name: Voicings: root–seventh–third
shells-fifth.e1.desc: Cmaj7, C7, Cm7 and Cm7b5 on strings 5, 3 and 2.

shells-fifth.e2.name: Voicings: root–third–seventh
shells-fifth.e2.desc: The same four chords on strings 5, 4 and 3.

shells-251.e1.name: Voicings: ii–V–I with shells
shells-251.e1.desc: Dm7, G7 and Cmaj7 by the nearest voicings; the bass string changes wherever the hand can stay.

shells-251.e2.name: Loop: ii–V–I in swing
shells-251.e2.desc: Shell voicings, four strokes to the bar. Change the key with the selector.

shells-251.e3.name: Loop: jazz blues with shells
shells-251.e3.desc: The whole jazz blues in F with shell voicings only.

drop2-top.e1.name: Voicings: drop 2 on strings 1-4
drop2-top.e1.desc: The four inversions of Cmaj7, C7, Cm7 and Cm7b5 up the neck.

drop2-middle.e1.name: Voicings: drop 2 on strings 2-5
drop2-middle.e1.desc: The four inversions of Gmaj7, G7, Gm7 and Gm7b5 up the neck.

drop2-251.e1.name: Voicings: ii–V–I with drop 2
drop2-251.e1.desc: Dm7, G7 and Cmaj7 by the nearest voicings. Pick the string set with the selector.

drop2-251.e2.name: Loop: ii–V–I drop 2 on strings 1-4
drop2-251.e2.desc: The microphone checks the top voice on beat one of each chord.

drop2-251.e3.name: Loop: ii–V–I drop 2 on strings 2-5
drop2-251.e3.desc: The same on the middle strings.

drop3.e1.name: Voicings: drop 3
drop3.e1.desc: The four inversions of Gmaj7, G7, Gm7 and Gm7b5 with the bass on string 6 or 5.

guide-tones.e1.name: Loop: jazz blues in two notes
guide-tones.e1.desc: Only the third and seventh of each chord on the D and G strings.

guide-tones.e2.name: Loop: ii–V–I in every key
guide-tones.e2.desc: Thirds and sevenths through the whole ii–V–I cycle.

comping-rhythm.e1.name: Loop: four to the bar
comping-rhythm.e1.desc: A jazz blues with shell voicings in Freddie Green style.

comping-rhythm.e2.name: Loop: bossa nova
comping-rhythm.e2.desc: Blue Bossa with drop 2 voicings in a bossa rhythm.

comping-standards.e1.name: Loop: three standards
comping-standards.e1.desc: Autumn Leaves, Rhythm changes and All the Things You Are with drop 2 voicings. The microphone checks the top voice.

ear-tonic.e1.name: Quiz: tonic, third or fifth
ear-tonic.e1.desc: A cadence in a random key, then one note. Which degree is it?

ear-tonic.e2.name: Play a note by ear
ear-tonic.e2.desc: After the cadence you hear the tonic, the third or the fifth. Find it on the fretboard and play it.

ear-degrees.e1.name: Quiz: major degrees
ear-degrees.e1.desc: A cadence, then one of the seven degrees of the major scale.

ear-degrees.e2.name: Play a degree by ear
ear-degrees.e2.desc: One note from the whole major scale: find it and play it.

ear-minor.e1.name: Quiz: minor degrees
ear-minor.e1.desc: A minor cadence, then one degree of the minor scale.

ear-minor.e2.name: Play a minor degree
ear-minor.e2.desc: One note from the minor scale: find it and play it.

ear-intervals-up.e1.name: Quiz: easy ascending intervals
ear-intervals-up.e1.desc: Thirds, the fourth, the fifth and the octave, from the lower note.

ear-intervals-all.e1.name: Quiz: all intervals
ear-intervals-all.e1.desc: From the minor second to the octave, up and down.

ear-intervals-all.e2.name: Play two notes by ear
ear-intervals-all.e2.desc: After the cadence you hear two notes: play them in the same order.

ear-intervals-harmonic.e1.name: Quiz: intervals played together
ear-intervals-harmonic.e1.desc: Two notes at once. Which interval is it?

ear-triads.e1.name: Quiz: triad quality
ear-triads.e1.desc: Major, minor, diminished or augmented, in voicings on different strings.

ear-sevenths.e1.name: Quiz: seventh chord quality
ear-sevenths.e1.desc: maj7, 7, m7 or m7b5, in drop 2 voicings.

ear-inversions.e1.name: Quiz: what is in the bass
ear-inversions.e1.desc: A major or minor triad: root, third or fifth in the bass?

ear-functions.e1.name: Quiz: chord function
ear-functions.e1.desc: A cadence, then one chord of the key: I, ii, iii, IV, V or vi?

ear-progressions.e1.name: Quiz: progression
ear-progressions.e1.desc: A cadence, then four chords. Which progression is it?

ear-echo.e1.name: Three-note phrases
ear-echo.e1.desc: Degrees 1–5 in major, mostly stepwise. Play each phrase after you hear it.

ear-echo.e2.name: Four-note phrases
ear-echo.e2.desc: The whole major scale, mostly stepwise, sometimes a leap.

ear-echo.e3.name: Minor phrases
ear-echo.e3.desc: Three notes from the minor scale.
